description: XPlane es un buen ejemplo de cómo conectar ciencia, ingeniería y creatividad para resolver un problema real. Somos Alejandro, Víctor y Eneko. We make records 😏
summary:
What does it really take to put something in space? Rocket Odyssey lets anyone find out, without solving a single equation.

You run a space agency with five clients: a university with $35M for its first satellite, a telecom operator that wants to connect a continent, and an agency dreaming of its own space station. Pick the payload, the orbit and the rocket, balance every dollar and every kilogram, and press “Launch!”.

This is not a game with made-up rules. Behind every launch is a simplified but real simulation. It uses the rocket equation applied stage by stage, launch vehicles based on real ones (from Electron to Saturn V), and the speed each orbit really needs. A good design reaches orbit. A bad one runs out of fuel, can’t lift its payload or flies its crew into the radiation belts, and the game shows exactly what happened and why. Fix it, launch again, and chase the one design that scores a perfect 100.

The physics stays under the hood, so players learn what real engineers learn: what works, what doesn’t, and why.
details:
Rocket Odyssey is a browser game in which players act as mission planners. Across five contracts, from a $35M university CubeSat to a $520M crewed orbital outpost, they choose a payload, an orbit and one of eight rockets. Live gauges show budget, mass and delta-v (the change in speed needed to reach orbit) as they go. Then they press “Launch!”. The game never blocks a bad design. The outcome is calculated with the real rocket equation, applied stage by stage, and the animation shows exactly that result. A debrief explains in plain language why the mission succeeded or failed and how to fix it.

The goal is to make space engineering approachable for students and beginners. Players learn trade-offs, staging and orbital energy by making mistakes safely, without having to study formulas.

The creativity lies in how the game teaches. Most space games are either detailed simulators that overwhelm beginners or simple builders where physics doesn’t matter. Rocket Odyssey sits in between: the physics is real, but players see its consequences, not its equations. Each contract is written as a client’s request, not a technical spec. “Zero signal interruptions” or “keep astronauts operating for several days” must be turned into engineering choices by the player. The launch is calculated first and animated second, so everything on screen is true to the design. Players watch a rocket run dry before reaching orbit, a payload too heavy to lift, or a crew exposed to radiation. Each payload type is drawn and deployed in its own way, and countdown beeps and engine sound add tension. Instead of “right” or “wrong”, the debrief explains each failure. The scoring turns success into a puzzle: several designs work, but only one scores 100, so players keep improving.

We considered accessibility from the start. The game follows international web accessibility standards (WCAG 2.1 AA). It can be played with a keyboard alone or with a screen reader, all information is also shown as text, and players who prefer less motion get a step-by-step timeline instead of the animation. The game is free and runs in any modern browser without an account.

It’s built in TypeScript with React, PixiJS and Hono, tested with Vitest and Playwright, and deployed with Docker on Railway. We developed it with the help of Claude Code.
